name: spinach ricotta
instructions:
A ricotta-and-greens pasta built on seared ricotta (or food-processed cottage cheese) + food-processor-chopped greens + cream + garlic. Nutmeg and red chili flakes carry the flavor — more so than the greens themselves (see notes). Dairy only — the vegan variant is retired (see the READ-ONLY reference log in notes; its concepts live on in [[chard-pickle-pasta]]).

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- pasta (rigatoni or penne — see PASTA SHAPE note)
- olive oil
- garlic
- ricotta cheese and/or cottage cheese (see notes on the swap)
- spinach, parsley, mixed greens (or really any greens — see notes)
- heavy whipping cream (as much as needed to bring the sauce together)
- nutmeg (to taste — critical, see notes)
- red chili flakes (to taste — critical, see notes)
- cayenne pepper
- lemon juice and lemon zest (to taste)
- pasta water (reserved from cooking)
- salt, black pepper

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. Cook the pasta in well-salted water. Reserve some pasta water before draining.
2. In a separate pan, cook the garlic in olive oil until fragrant (don't brown).
3. SEAR/COOK THE RICOTTA (OR FOOD-PROCESSED COTTAGE CHEESE): add the ricotta (or cottage cheese run through a food processor to smooth it out) to the garlicky oil. Let it cook against the hot pan — searing gives it a slightly toasted, more concentrated flavor rather than reading as raw cheese.
4. Chop the greens (spinach + parsley + mixed greens) in a food processor. Fold them in after the ricotta has seared.
5. Add heavy cream as necessary to bring it together into a proper sauce.
6. Season with nutmeg, red chili flakes, and cayenne — all to taste. Nutmeg and chili flakes are the load-bearing flavors here (see notes).
7. Finish with lemon juice and lemon zest to taste.
8. Add the cooked pasta and enough reserved pasta water to loosen the sauce and get it to coat the pasta.
9. Salt and black pepper to taste.

OPTIONAL BAKED FORMAT: transfer the sauced pasta to a baking dish, top generously with mozzarella and/or monterrey jack, and bake until melted and golden — see the BAKED note. This is the direction to develop next (see NEXT FOCUS).
notes:
=== NUTMEG AND CHILI FLAKES ARE CRITICAL — MORE SO THAN THE GREENS ===

The greens carry visual/textural weight but the FLAVOR of the dish is nutmeg + red chili flakes. Without them the sauce reads flat and generic-creamy-cheese. With them it reads as a proper composed dish. Add both to taste — don't skimp. If you're going to under-do anything in this recipe, let it be the greens; if you're going to over-do anything, let it be the nutmeg and chili flakes.

=== SEAR/COOK THE RICOTTA — DON'T LEAVE IT RAW ===

Cooking the ricotta (or food-processed cottage cheese) against the hot garlicky pan is a real technique step, not just heating. Searing gives the cheese a slightly toasted, more concentrated flavor that reads as an actual cooked component rather than as a raw dairy dollop stirred in. Skip this and the sauce reads flat and dairy-forward without the cheese pulling its weight.

=== RICOTTA OR FOOD-PROCESSED COTTAGE CHEESE — INTERCHANGEABLE ===

Either works. Ricotta is smoother out of the tub. Cottage cheese needs a food processor pass first to smooth out the curds — unprocessed cottage cheese would give you visible grainy curds in the sauce, which reads wrong. Same swap-friendly cheese-role framing as tomato-tart's bulk cheese role.

=== CREAM AS NEEDED FOR A REAL SAUCE ===

How much cream depends on how the ricotta + greens land — sometimes the mixture is already spreadable, sometimes it needs real thinning. Add enough cream to bring it to a sauce consistency that will coat the pasta once you toss with pasta water. Not a fixed amount; go by feel.

PASTA WATER TO LOOSEN AT THE END: reserve pasta water before draining. Add enough to bring the sauce to coating consistency after the pasta goes in. Standard italian pasta-sauce move — the starchy water helps the sauce cling.

=== PASTA SHAPE — RIGATONI AND PENNE ===

RIGATONI and PENNE — the tubes hold the chunky ricotta base cleanly, and they're especially good when the dish is BAKED (below). Fettuccine is edible but not the pick; spaghetti reads wrong against a chunky sauce.

=== UNLIKE PESTO — CAN BE BAKED IN THE OVEN WITH LOTS OF CHEESE ===

Unlike pesto (which is served raw / warm-off-heat), spinach ricotta CAN be baked in the oven with a generous cheese top layer — the ricotta base holds up to the bake and takes a proper melted-cheese crust.

CHEESE FOR THE BAKED APPLICATION: MOZZARELLA or MONTERREY JACK are the more common picks — meltier, stretchier, more of a baked-pasta / casserole register. Parmesan works too but reads less traditional for this application. If you want the italian-classical bake, mozzarella. If you want more of an american-comfort register, monterrey jack. Combine both if you can't decide.

=== NEXT FOCUS — BAKING / LASAGNE ===

The development direction for this recipe is the BAKED family: baked rigatoni/penne with the cheese top, and eventually lasagne with the ricotta-and-greens base as a filling layer. The stovetop pasta version above is settled; the oven applications are where the open work is.

=== VARIANT C (STUB) — TOMATO PASTE + HEAVY CREAM + LOOSE-LEAF SPINACH ===

Stub. Build on the base above, then apply two changes:

1. TOMATO PASTE + HEAVY CREAM added to the base — pushes the flavor profile toward tomato-cream (vodka-sauce-adjacent) rather than the plain ricotta-and-greens direction.
2. LOOSE-LEAF SPINACH rather than food-processor-chopped spinach. Whole leaves wilted in rather than dispersed through the base. Reads chunkier and greener; different visual and mouthfeel.

Untested / stub. Log when tried.

RAW FRESH TOMATO chopped up and folded into the finished dish works well as a secondary addition. Fresh (not cooked, not canned). Skip if you don't have a ripe tomato; not required.

=== GREENS — REALLY ANYTHING WORKS ===

Spinach, parsley, and mixed greens as the canonical trio. Chop/pulse in a food processor before folding in — food-processed greens distribute through the sauce evenly rather than sitting as leafy strands.

=== DON'T USE A BLENDER — FOOD PROCESSOR, KEEP IT COARSE ===

Blenders are wrong for this dish (and for spinach-plus-white-cheese preparations generally) for two reasons:

1. COLOR — NICKELODEON GREEN SLIME: high-shear blending fully ruptures the spinach cells and disperses the chlorophyll evenly through the white cheese base. Ends up as a weird pale-green goo that reads un-food-like. Food processor pulses leave spinach in visible flecks against the white base, which reads correct.

2. TEXTURE — KEEP IT COARSE: this sauce should read as ricotta-with-chopped-greens, not as a smooth green sauce. Food processor pulses let you stop at coarse; blender over-smooths. The visible-flecks-of-green + visible-curds-of-cheese texture is what makes it feel like a proper italian ricotta preparation rather than a pureed cream sauce.

If a blender is your only tool: pulse in short bursts and stop early. Expect the color problem regardless.

=== NO NUTS ===

Dairy ricotta / cottage cheese + cream carries the body; nuts just clutter. All nuts clashing (cashews earned their keep only in the retired vegan variant below).

=== RETIRED VEGAN VARIANT — READ-ONLY REFERENCE LOG ===

The vegan variant (Beth Hornback / Pass the Plants base: silken tofu + soaked cashews + spinach + basil + miso + nooch, raw-blended) was developed extensively and is now RETIRED from this recipe. The book is closed for three reasons:

1. NO GOOD VEGAN SPINACH RICOTTA WITHOUT A GOOD VEGAN PARMESAN: the ricotta role can be landed, but these green-sauce pastas are hard to eat without parmesan, and the DIY vegan parms all run on the same nooch/miso/cashew axis as the base — sprinkling the sauce on the sauce.
2. BETTER USES FOR SILKEN TOFU: the silken-tofu slot is more valuable elsewhere (see [[chard-pickle-pasta]], the direct descendant).
3. THE HERBS SWING IT INTO PESTO TERRITORY: leaning on basil/fine herbs for flavor makes it a creamy vegan basil pesto — which is a SEPARATE recipe, not a variant of this one. (And if herbal extraction is the goal, cream in a blender extracts more herb flavor than a tofu base ever will.)

LESSONS PRESERVED FOR LATER USE (all validated by experiment during the vegan-variant era):
- SETTLED BASE: silken tofu + soaked cashews, ~2:1 tofu-to-cashews by mass. Firm tofu closed out — silken's creaminess + cashew body is the texture. Soak cashews 30+ min warm water or they leave grit.
- SILENT INGREDIENTS RULE: miso paste (~1 tsp) + nutritional yeast (~2 tbsp) should NOT be tasteable — background umami only. If you can identify them, you overdid it. Fix mildness with the proper seasonings, not more miso.
- CALIBRATE UP: olive oil + lemon juice/zest — the consistent under-dos. Push further than feels natural.
- MISO GOES IN THE FOOD-PROCESSOR PHASE: low-liquid recipe; folded in late it stays as concentrated blobs.
- WARM, DON'T SIMMER blended-tofu sauces: they don't thicken, don't caramelize, and get grainy if pushed.
- WHOLE WHEAT SPAGHETTI for the creamy-oily tofu base — its nutty chew stands up to the miso/nooch/cashew register in a way refined flour doesn't (the dairy version keeps its tubes).
- CORIANDER over nutmeg as the spice for tofu-base versions — its citrusy-warm character suits the oil + lemon axis; nutmeg leans on the dairy register.
- PORCINI POWDER breaks up the miso/nooch glutamate monotone with a different (woodsy) savory.
- CASHEWS THE ONLY VALID NUT in the tofu base; pepitas or no-nuts-double-tofu are Beth's allergy subs.
- NISHA VORA'S ALL-CASHEW VEGAN RICOTTA (Rainbow Plant Life) was the other reference point — pickle juice + onion powder + black pepper giving a tangy-allium register. Her full recipe and the ideas taken from it now live in [[chard-pickle-pasta]].

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- [[chard-pickle-pasta]]: the descendant of the retired vegan variant — the silken+cashew base redirected at swiss chard + the Nisha pickle-juice/onion-powder axis, seasoned with cumin in the anglo-germanic register (no cheese there — its glutamate budget is already spent).
- [[mushroomed-lentils-british]]: uses cashews + miso + nutritional yeast in a similar umami stack, but as filling in a savory-baked log.
original_chef: Mine. (The retired vegan variant was Beth Hornback's, Pass the Plants — see the read-only log in notes.)
